interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: When Small Models Are Right for Wrong Reasons: Process Verification for Trustworthy Agents
papers.abstract: Deploying small language models (7-9B parameters) as autonomous agents requires trust in their reasoning, not just their outputs. We reveal a critical reliability crisis: 50-69\% of correct answers from these models contain fundamentally flawed reasoning -- a ``Right-for-Wrong-Reasons'' phenomenon invisible to standard accuracy metrics. Through analysis of 10,734 reasoning traces across three models and diverse tasks, we introduce the Reasoning Integrity Score (RIS), a process-based metric validated with substantial inter-rater agreement ($κ=0.657$). Conventional practices are challenged by our findings: while retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) significantly improves reasoning integrity (Cohen's $d=0.23$--$0.93$), meta-cognitive interventions like self-critique often harm performance ($d=-0.14$ to $-0.33$) in small models on the evaluated tasks. Mechanistic analysis reveals RAG succeeds by grounding calculations in external evidence, reducing errors by 7.6\%, while meta-cognition amplifies confusion without sufficient model capacity. To enable deployment, verification capabilities are distilled into a neural classifier achieving 0.86 F1-score with 100$\times$ speedup. These results underscore the necessity of process-based verification for trustworthy agents: accuracy alone is dangerously insufficient when models can be right for entirely wrong reasons.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses reasoning integrity in LLM agents, which is critical for trustworthy scientific workflows and automated research agents.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether small language models (7-9B parameters) can be trusted when they give correct answers, revealing that 50-69% of correct answers contain flawed reasoning. The authors introduce a Reasoning Integrity Score (RIS) to measure process quality, finding that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves reasoning integrity while self-critique harms it. For astronomy, this matters because deploying LLM agents for tasks like literature review or data analysis requires confidence in their reasoning, not just final outputs. A concrete workflow would be using RAG to ground an agent's reasoning in known astronomical catalogs or papers before it writes analysis code. A caveat is that the study uses small models and generic tasks, so transferability to specialized astronomical reasoning needs verification.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the Reasoning Integrity Score (RIS) methodology could be adapted to evaluate reasoning traces in astronomical data analysis workflows
Look for the specific RAG implementation details and whether they use external knowledge bases that could be replaced with astronomical databases
Examine the types of reasoning failures (e.g., arithmetic, factual, logical) to see which are most relevant to scientific reasoning tasks

papers.title: S1-MMAlign: A Large-Scale, Multi-Disciplinary Dataset for Scientific Figure-Text Understanding
papers.authors: He Wang, Longteng Guo, Pengkang Huo, Xuanxu Lin, Yichen Yuan, Jie Jiang, Jing Liu
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning has revolutionized general domain tasks, yet its application in scientific discovery is hindered by the profound semantic gap between complex scientific imagery and sparse textual descriptions. We present S1-MMAlign, a large-scale, multi-disciplinary multimodal dataset comprising over 15.5 million high-quality image-text pairs derived from 2.5 million open-access scientific papers. Spanning disciplines from physics and biology to engineering, the dataset captures diverse visual modalities including experimental setups, heatmaps, and microscopic imagery. To address the pervasive issue of weak alignment in raw scientific captions, we introduce an AI-ready semantic enhancement pipeline that leverages advanced multimodal large language models to recaption images, by synthesizing comprehensive context from paper abstracts and the citation contexts of corresponding figures. Technical validation confirms that our enhancement pipeline markedly improves data quality via reduced SciBERT pseudo-perplexity and enhanced CLIP image-text alignment, while also significantly boosting multimodal large language models performance in zero-shot scientific captioning, multi-domain scientific reasoning, and visual instruction tuning. S1-MMAlign provides a pivotal foundational resource for cross-modal scientific understanding in the AI for Science era, supporting the development of scientific foundation models and a wide range of downstream scientific intelligence applications. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScienceOne-AI/S1-MMAlign.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly provides a large-scale multimodal dataset of scientific figures and text, which is highly relevant for building multimodal models for astronomy (e.g., matching JWST images to captions or literature).
papers.Short digest: This paper aims to solve the problem of weak alignment between scientific figures and their captions, which hinders multimodal AI for science. The authors create S1-MMAlign, a dataset of 15.5 million image-text pairs from 2.5 million open-access papers, and use a multimodal LLM to rewrite captions by incorporating context from the paper abstract and citation contexts. For astronomy, this could enable models that understand figures like JWST images or spectra alongside their descriptions, aiding literature review or automated captioning. A concrete workflow would be fine-tuning a vision-language model on this dataset to retrieve relevant figures from a paper given a science question. A caveat is that the dataset covers many disciplines, so astronomy-specific performance may need validation, and the recaptioning pipeline may introduce its own biases.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the distribution of astronomy/astrophysics papers in the dataset and whether captions for typical JWST figures (images, spectra) are well-represented.
Look for quantitative results on zero-shot scientific captioning or retrieval tasks that include astronomy examples.
Examine the recaptioning pipeline's validation metrics (SciBERT PPL, CLIP alignment) to assess if quality improvements are consistent across domains.

papers.title: Deep Delta Learning
papers.authors: Yifan Zhang, Yifeng Liu, Mengdi Wang, Quanquan Gu
papers.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Transformer residual streams evolve by additive accumulation: each layer appends a feature update to a shared hidden state, but has no direct mechanism for replacing content that has become obsolete or conflicting. We introduce Deep Delta Learning (DDL), a residual update rule that preserves the identity path while giving every layer the ability to selectively rewrite residual content. DDL reads the current state along a learned direction, compares it with a learned target value, and writes back a gated correction along the same direction. When the gate is closed, the update reduces to the identity; when the gate is fully open, the selected component is overwritten, yielding a depth-wise delta-rule generalization of standard residual addition. We integrate DDL in decoder-only language models with both scalar and expanded residual states, while keeping attention and MLP sublayers at the original compute width. Controlled pretraining and downstream evaluations show that residual rewrite operations improve language modeling quality relative to pure additive accumulation introduced in ResNet, suggesting that a learned delta-rule update is an effective mechanism for managing Transformer residual streams.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper introduces a novel residual update rule for transformers, which could improve LLM training for scientific applications.
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes Deep Delta Learning (DDL), a new residual update rule for transformers that allows layers to selectively rewrite content rather than just additively accumulate. The method preserves the identity path while enabling gated corrections, improving language modeling quality. For astronomy, better LLMs could enhance automated literature review, data analysis, and scientific reasoning. However, the paper is focused on language modeling pretraining and does not directly address astronomical data. The technique is a general improvement to transformer architecture, not a specific tool for JWST analysis.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if DDL is evaluated on tasks relevant to scientific reasoning or long-context understanding.
Look for any analysis of how the rewrite mechanism affects factual accuracy or hallucination.

papers.title: Context Collapse: In-Context Learning and Model Collapse
papers.abstract: This thesis investigates two key phenomena in large language models (LLMs): in-context learning (ICL) and model collapse. We study ICL in a linear transformer with tied weights trained on linear regression tasks, and show that minimising the in-context loss leads to a phase transition in the learned parameters. Above a critical context length, the solution develops a skew-symmetric component. We prove this by reducing the forward pass of the linear transformer under weight tying to preconditioned gradient descent, and then analysing the optimal preconditioner. This preconditioner includes a skew-symmetric component, which induces a rotation of the gradient direction. For model collapse, we use martingale and random walk theory to analyse simplified settings - linear regression and Gaussian fitting - under both replacing and cumulative data regimes. We strengthen existing results by proving almost sure convergence, showing that collapse occurs unless the data grows sufficiently fast or is retained over time. Finally, we introduce the notion of context collapse: a degradation of context during long generations, especially in chain-of-thought reasoning. This concept links the dynamics of ICL with long-term stability challenges in generative models.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper studies in-context learning and model collapse in LLMs, relevant to understanding LLM behavior for scientific use.
papers.Short digest: This thesis investigates in-context learning and model collapse in large language models. It shows that minimizing in-context loss leads to a phase transition in learned parameters, and that model collapse occurs unless data grows sufficiently fast. For astronomy, understanding model collapse is important when using LLMs for iterative scientific analysis or chain-of-thought reasoning. However, the paper is theoretical and does not provide practical tools for astronomical data analysis. The results are about fundamental LLM dynamics, not specific to astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the paper provides practical guidelines for avoiding model collapse in scientific applications.
Look for any experiments on long-context reasoning tasks relevant to scientific workflows.

papers.title: Vision-Language Reasoning for Geolocalization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.authors: Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Ling Chen, Ke Xu, Tao Cheng, Jun Wang
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models have opened up new possibilities for reasoning-driven image geolocalization. However, existing approaches often rely on synthetic reasoning annotations or external image retrieval, which can limit interpretability and generalizability. In this paper, we present Geo-R, a retrieval-free framework that uncovers structured reasoning paths from existing ground-truth coordinates and optimizes geolocation accuracy via reinforcement learning. We propose the Chain of Region, a rule-based hierarchical reasoning paradigm that generates precise, interpretable supervision by mapping GPS coordinates to geographic entities (e.g., country, province, city) without relying on model-generated or synthetic labels. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight reinforcement learning strategy with coordinate-aligned rewards based on Haversine distance, enabling the model to refine predictions through spatially meaningful feedback. Our approach bridges structured geographic reasoning with direct spatial supervision, yielding improved localization accuracy, stronger generalization, and more transparent inference. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of Geo-R, establishing a new retrieval-free paradigm for scalable and interpretable image geolocalization. To facilitate further research and ensure reproducibility, both the model and code will be made publicly available.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper uses vision-language models and reinforcement learning for geolocalization, which could inspire multimodal reasoning for astronomical data.
papers.Short digest: This paper presents Geo-R, a retrieval-free framework for image geolocalization using vision-language models and reinforcement learning. It introduces Chain of Region, a hierarchical reasoning paradigm that maps GPS coordinates to geographic entities, and uses Haversine distance as reward. For astronomy, the approach of combining visual reasoning with structured spatial knowledge could be adapted for astronomical source localization or classification. However, the paper is focused on Earth imagery and does not address astronomical data. The reinforcement learning strategy for spatial reasoning is the most transferable concept.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the Chain of Region paradigm could be adapted for celestial coordinate systems.
Look for any discussion of generalization to non-Earth imagery or scientific domains.
